title: Hammocks for a free factor agree with ordinary inversion
statement: Use simplicial categories and weak homotopy equivalences as in [lem-coef-coherent-nerve-comparison]. For an ordinary category $P$ with a wide subcategory $T$, write $H(P,T)(x,y)_k$ for reduced commutative rectangular zigzags with $k+1$ rows from $x$ to $y$: vertical arrows point down and lie in $T$, endpoint vertical arrows are identities, each horizontal column has uniform direction, leftward arrows lie in $T$, directions alternate, and no column is entirely identities. Include the length-zero diagram when $x=y$. Operators delete or repeat rows and then reduce by deleting identity columns and composing adjacent columns with the same direction. Composition concatenates and reduces. For a simplicial pair $(A,U)$ with a fixed object set, $\operatorname{diag}H(A,U)(x,y)_n=H(A_n,U_n)(x,y)_n$, with both simplicial operators applied together. Let $O$ be a small set and let $D,V$ be free ordinary categories with object set $O$: each has a chosen set of nonidentity generating arrows, and every arrow has a unique finite composable word in those generators, with the empty word representing an identity. Let $P=D*_O V$ be their coproduct among categories with object set $O$ and functors fixing $O$, and identify $V$ with its canonical wide subcategory of $P$. Let $P[V^{-1}]$ be the category with the same objects obtained by adjoining inverses to arrows of $V$, subject to the composition and inverse relations. Regard its mapping sets as discrete simplicial sets. Sending a hammock to the composite of any row in $P[V^{-1}]$, using inverses for leftward arrows, defines a simplicial functor $H(P,V)\to P[V^{-1}]$ which is the identity on objects and induces a weak homotopy equivalence on every mapping simplicial set. This functor is natural for functors of such pairs preserving $V$; no chosen generators need be preserved by these functors.

source.place: Dwyer–Kan, Calculating simplicial localizations, Comparison Lemma 2.3, printed p.20; proof in Section 5.8, printed pp.24–25 No Stacks tag states this simplicial-localization result.

proof.text: The row-product assignment is well defined. In a reduced hammock, orient each rightward horizontal arrow as it is written and each leftward arrow by the inverse of its arrow in $V$. Commutativity of every rectangle and the fact that each vertical arrow belongs to $V$ imply that the products along adjacent rows agree in $P[V^{-1}]$; the endpoint vertical arrows are identities, so all row products equal. Deleting or repeating a row and then reducing identity columns or adjacent columns preserves this value, and horizontal concatenation multiplies the values. Thus the assignment is a simplicial functor, identity on objects, and is natural under functors preserving $V$. The meaning of weak homotopy equivalence on mapping simplicial sets is the one in [lem-coef-coherent-nerve-comparison].

source.place: Definition 2.1 and the row-product map in Comparison Lemma 2.3, printed pp.19–20

proof.text: Apply [lem-coef-free-factor-hammock-pushout] with $W=V$. It gives $H(P,V)=D*_O H(V,V)$ and $P[V^{-1}]=D*_O V[V^{-1}]$, and identifies the comparison with $D*_O$ of the whole-category comparison. The last clause of [lem-coef-fixed-object-simplicial-free-calculus], applied to the identity of the discrete simplicial category $D$ and the whole-category comparison, preserves mappingwise weak equivalences under this free product over $O$. Thus it suffices to prove the comparison for $(C,C)$ with $C$ free. Separate the generating graph into its connected components: every arrow and every row of a hammock stays in one such component. For objects in distinct components both the hammock set and ordinary-localization Hom set are empty. There are no object pairs if $O$ is empty. It remains to treat a nonempty connected free category.

For a nonempty connected free $C$, choose a lift $\widetilde x$ of $x$ in the covering category of [lem-coef-free-factor-hammock-universal-cover-reduction]. Its generating graph is an oriented tree and its nerve is contractible. The stated simplicial isomorphism decomposes $H(C,C)(x,y)$ as the disjoint union of $H(\widetilde C,\widetilde C)(\widetilde x,\widetilde y)$ over lifts of $y$. Accordingly it is enough to prove that the mapping simplicial sets for the free category on an arbitrary oriented tree are nonempty and weakly contractible. The covering lemma applies only to $(C,C)$; it is never applied to a pair with a surviving $D$ factor.

Fix a vertex $x$ and a finite signed word $w$. First let the oriented tree $T$ be finite. Induct on its number of edges. For the singleton tree the fixed-word category of [def-coef-zigzag-homotopy-calculus] has one object and only its identity, even for the empty word, so its nerve is a point. Otherwise a maximal simple path has two leaf endpoints: an extra neighbour would either extend the path or form a cycle. Choose a leaf $l\ne x$ and delete it, leaving a tree with one fewer edge. Apply [lem-coef-tree-leaf-zigzag-retraction] with both endpoints $x$. Its functors are a retraction with a natural transformation in one direction between the other composite and the identity. By [lem-coef-nerve-natural-homotopy-equivalence] the two nerves are homotopy equivalent. The induction hypothesis therefore proves that $NZ_w^{C_T}(x,x)$ is weakly contractible.

source.place: Section 5.8(iii), printed p.25: finite-tree contraction via leaf collapse

proof.text: For an arbitrary small oriented tree $T$, [lem-coef-tree-zigzag-finite-subtree-colimit] identifies $NZ_w^{C_T}(x,x)$ with the degreewise colimit over the small nonempty filtered poset $\mathcal F_x(T)$. Every finite-subtree collapse map $NZ_w^{C_S}(x,x)\to\Delta^0$ is a weak homotopy equivalence by the preceding induction. These maps form a natural transformation to the constant point diagram. Apply [lem-coef-filtered-colimit-weak-equivalences]. The colimit of the constant point diagram is a point: every representative is the unique point of some index, and a common upper bound identifies any two representatives. Consequently $NZ_w^{C_T}(x,x)$ is weakly contractible.

source.place: Section 5.8(iii): explicit rooted-leaf induction, followed by finite-subtree filtered colimits; natural-transformations-on-nerves input is cited separately.

proof.text: By [lem-coef-hammock-graph-colimit-presentation], the fixed-word nerves $NZ^C_w(x,x)$ form a proper diagram on the small signed-word category, and their colimit is $H(C,C)(x,x)$. Collapse every fixed-word nerve to a point. The constant point diagram is proper: all injection maps are identities and the two-image intersection condition is the equality $\{*\}=\{*\}\cap\{*\}$. The collapse maps are weak homotopy equivalences by the preceding step, so [lem-coef-proper-word-colimit-invariance] makes the map on colimits a weak homotopy equivalence. The signed-word category has an initial empty word, so its constant point diagram has colimit a point. It follows that $H(C,C)(x,x)$ is weakly contractible.

For arbitrary vertices $x,y$ of the tree, follow the finite undirected path from $x$ to $y$. All its oriented generating arrows belong to the distinguished category $C$. With source fixed at $x$, each such arrow induces a weak equivalence between the successive target mapping spaces by [lem-coef-hammock-inverted-arrow-actions], in the forward or backward direction according to its orientation. Starting with the weakly contractible $H(C,C)(x,x)$, this finite chain of weak equivalences shows $H(C,C)(x,y)$ is nonempty and weakly contractible. By the cover decomposition above, every component of the original $H(C,C)(x,y)$ is weakly contractible. Finally [lem-coef-hammock-components-localization] says that the row-product comparison induces the bijection from these components to $C[C^{-1}](x,y)$, so it is a weak homotopy equivalence to that discrete simplicial set. Step 2 now gives the required free-factor comparison.

The constructions use only composition, identities, the chosen wide subcategory and inversion of its arrows. Applying a functor of free-factor pairs preserving $V$ sends every row, vertical square, reduction and row product to the corresponding one in the target, so the comparison is natural and the composition law is respected. This completes the stated weak equivalence and its naturality.

proof_origin.place: Comparison Lemma 2.3, Sections 3.1–3.3 and 4.1–5.8, read online; finite-subtree and proper-word colimit arguments written out here. Paper not archived under literature/.
